content:
Melbourne is in its sixth month of lockdown, the longest in the world. I'm in Adelaide, where restrictions have been lighter and the atmosphere is identical - a pervasive, low-grade sense of being managed. Told where you can go. Told who you can see. Told what counts as an essential reason to leave your house.

I comply, and that's worth stating up front. I wear the mask, I check in, I follow the rules. I write this from a position of recognition rather than defiance, because I recognise this energy. It has happened before.

In the late 1960s and early 1970s an entire generation looked at the machinery of the state - the draft sending young men to die in Vietnam, the surveillance monitoring domestic dissent, the censorship controlling what could be said and shown and thought - and arrived at a collective realisation that the government had no right to any of it. The counterculture was many things, chaotic and naive and self-indulgent among them, and at its core it was a recognition that the state had claimed authority over the bodies and minds of its citizens that it had never earned.

I feel that energy now. Different direction, different clothes, same essential vibration. The state has decided what you may do with your body, where you may take it, who you may bring it near. The justification is public health and the justification has merit. I'm no COVID denier. The virus is real, the hospitals are real, the dead are real.

The mechanism is the same all the same. The state claims authority over your physical person, and most people comply because compliance is the default rather than because they've weighed evidence and reached an independent conclusion. Questioning authority in the middle of a crisis feels irresponsible, or dangerous, or simply exhausting.

I hold a principle I suspect is less common than I'd like: you should be permitted to do with your body whatever you choose, provided you don't harm others. That's the foundational premise of liberal democracy stated plainly, and in practice we abandon it reflexively the moment an authority figure says it's necessary.

**Being Direct About This**

I want to talk about drugs, and specifically about psychedelics, and I want to be direct, because directness is the only approach that respects the subject.

I've taken DMT, in a setting that was deliberate and considered and treated with the seriousness the substance demands. No party was involved and nothing about it was recreational. I won't describe the experience in full, because it resists language in ways that make description nearly dishonest. I'll say it was among the most significant perceptual events of my life. Significant rather than enjoyable, in the way a door opening onto a landscape you didn't know existed is significant.

What I experienced was a way of perceiving I hadn't known was available. The filters through which I normally take in reality - the assumptions, the categories, the unconscious architecture of perception - became visible as filters. I could see them. I could see they were constructions rather than fixed features of the world, and that the world behind them was larger and stranger and more intricate than the constructions allowed.

I came back through the door and the door closed, and the world I returned to looked different. Nothing in the world had changed. I had seen, briefly and with overwhelming clarity, how thoroughly my normal perception was managed and curated and filtered through assumptions so deeply embedded I'd mistaken them for reality.

That experience made me think harder about why these substances are illegal. The official justification is public health - they're dangerous, addictive, harmful - and the trouble with that story is that it doesn't survive contact with the evidence.

Psilocybin has lower toxicity than aspirin. LSD has never been conclusively linked to a single overdose death. DMT is produced endogenously by the human brain. The clinical literature now emerging from Johns Hopkins and Imperial College London and elsewhere consistently finds therapeutic benefit for depression, PTSD, addiction and end-of-life anxiety. The substances classified as most dangerous are, on the evidence, among the least harmful.

Meanwhile alcohol kills thousands of Australians every year and tobacco kills more, and both are legal and regulated and taxed and sold at every corner shop. The scheduling of substances here, as in most Western countries, bears no relationship to their actual harm profile. It bears a relationship to something else.

**What the Timing Tells You**

The timing of prohibition is instructive. Psychedelics were legal in the United States through the early 1960s, used in clinical research and administered therapeutically. They were criminalised in 1970 under the Controlled Substances Act - the same year the counterculture peaked, the same year opposition to Vietnam reached critical mass, the same year the political establishment faced its most sustained challenge since the labour movements of the early twentieth century.

John Ehrlichman, Nixon's domestic policy advisor, said this in a 1994 interview: the campaign had two enemies, the antiwar left and Black people. They couldn't make it illegal to be against the war or to be Black. They could associate the antiwar movement with marijuana and Black communities with heroin, criminalise both, and disrupt those communities. Did they know they were lying about the drugs? Of course they did.

So the war on drugs was designed as a tool of political control, explicitly, by the admission of the people who designed it. The substances were banned for their association with people questioning authority, and the pharmacology never entered into it.

Fifty years on, the framework persists. The scheduling remains. In Australia, possession of psilocybin can bring imprisonment - for a substance less toxic than the paracetamol in your medicine cabinet, currently used in clinical trials at major universities, produced by mushrooms that grow wild in Australian paddocks.

The question I keep asking, and the one the lockdowns have sharpened, is why we trust them.

Not this government specifically. Government as an institution. The entity claiming authority over our bodies and minds, the substances we may ingest, the places we may go, the people we may see - an entity with an extensive, documented, undeniable history of lying, manipulating, and pursuing institutional interests under the banner of public welfare.

None of this makes me an anarchist. Coordination is necessary, rules are necessary, some authority is required for a society to function at all. What I'm arguing for is a considerably more sceptical posture towards governmental claims than most citizens maintain, and I'm arguing that the default of compliance is habitual rather than earned. It's the residue of an education system and a media environment that treat authority as legitimate until proven otherwise, when the historical record suggests the reverse.

**The Auditor**

There's a technology approaching that could change this dynamic, and I find it genuinely exciting. Large language models are advancing rapidly, and within years these systems will be capable of something that has never existed: real-time, comprehensive, incorruptible accountability.

Imagine a system with access to all government communications, budget allocations and policy outcomes. A system that can't be bribed or captured or threatened, that doesn't forget, whose sole function is to compare what governments say they're doing with what they're actually doing, and to publish the comparison instantly without editorial interference.

To be clear, algorithms should make no policy decisions. What I'm describing is more modest and more powerful - AI serving as a permanent auditor of the people who do make them. An alignment harness for the government rather than for the machine. A mechanism making dishonesty structurally visible, if not structurally impossible.

The alignment problem in AI safety, ensuring intelligent systems pursue the goals we intend, has a mirror image in governance: ensuring powerful institutions pursue the public interest rather than their own. We've been working on the governance version for centuries with constitutions and courts and a free press. None has fully succeeded, and all can be captured or corrupted or circumvented.

An AI auditor might succeed where those have partly failed, and not because these systems are inherently trustworthy, which they aren't. Because a system designed specifically for transparency, with the right architecture and constraints, could sustain a form of accountability human institutions never have.

That requires solving alignment for the auditor itself, which is far from trivial. A misaligned system with access to all government data would be extraordinarily dangerous. The possibility exists all the same, and in a world where governments have shown across centuries that they can't be trusted to police themselves, a non-human mechanism for enforcing honesty deserves serious attention.

The lockdown taught me something I'd suspected without fully feeling. The state will control your body if you let it and your mind if it can. The substances that expand perception are banned. The substances that narrow it are sold at every corner shop. None of that is an accident, and the question for the next decade is whether the most powerful technology ever built deepens that control or finally makes it transparent.

I know which outcome I want. I don't know which we'll get, and I'd rather more people were watching for the difference.
